newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen denies Saudi dissident establishing presence.
newsitem.headline: Yemen denies Saudi dissident establishing presence.

text.p: A Yemeni official on Saturday denied an exiled Saudi Arabian dissident, named by Washington as a prime suspect in bombings against U.S. targets in Saudi Arabia which killed 26, had gained a foothold in the country.
"There is no truth in reports carried by Reuters that (Osama) bin Laden is present or has gained a foothold in Yemen," said the official.
"Yemen will not allow its territories to become a launch pad for opposition activity against any brotherly or friendly country," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

Reuters quoted Arab diplomatic and Western intelligence sources in Sanaa on Friday as saying an advance party of bin Laden's supporters had established cells in Yemen, which shares a disputed border with Saudi Arabia.

The sources would not say whether they had evidence that bin Laden himself had arrived in Yemen or was still in Afghanistan, his base since last year when he was forced to leave Sudan under Saudi pressure.
"Yemen rejects and condemns terrorism and fundamentalism in all its forms and shapes regardless of its origin," the Yemeni official said.

In Islamabad, Afghan ambassador Mufti Masoom Afghani, a member of the purist Islamic Taleban militia, told a news conference bin Laden had been told not to use Afghanistan as a base for actions against any country, including Saudi Arabia.
"He has promised not to use our soil," Afghani said, without denying bin Laden's presence in his country.

Asked if the Taleban would consider deporting him to Saudi Arabia in exchange for a seat at the Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC), holding a summit in Islamabad on Sunday, he said neither the OIC nor Saudi Arabia had made any such offer.
"We don't have to think (about it) now," he added.

Bin Laden has been based near the eastern Afghan city of Jalalabad before and after the Taleban captured the area in September. A Reuter journalist in Jalalabad who requested an interview with him on Saturday was told to wait for an answer.

Bin Laden, a multi-millionaire financier stripped of his Saudi citizenship because of his activities against the royal family, has threatened to wage a holy war on "crusader" U.S. forces in the homeland of Islam.
He financed and commanded thousands of so-called Arab Afghans -- Islamic warriors from Saudi Arabia and other Arab states in the 1980s Afghan war against the Soviet Union.
U.S. officials last October branded him as a prime suspect in the two bombings which also wounded more than 400 people in 1995 and 1996.
Bin Laden denied involvement in the bombings but said they were warnings that the United States should withdraw its forces from Saudi Arabia.

Four Saudis were executed last year for the first blast. Saudi and U.S. investigations into the second bombing in eastern Saudi Arabia last June are continuing. No evidence connecting bin Laden to that explosion has been published.

An Arabic newspaper published in London, al-Quds al-Arabi, in November quoted bin Laden as saying in an interview that he was considering moving to Yemen, irrespective of whether the Yemeni government agreed.
